sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Testing is a first-class citizen in Go. The standard library ships testing, benchmarking, and example-based documentation in a single package. Interviewers expect Go engineers to know idiomatic patterns—table-driven tests, subtests with t.Run, TestMain for setup/teardown—because these appear in virtually every Go codebase. Demonstrating fluency signals that you write maintainable, production-quality code.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Go tests are just functions with the signature func TestXxx(t *testing.T). Everything else—assertions, mocks, containers—is built on top of that. Think in three rings: (1) Unit tests: pure functions, no I/O, fast. (2) Integration tests: real databases or HTTP servers, use build tags (+integration) or TestMain to control execution. (3) Benchmark tests: func BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B)—run with go test -bench=. to measure nanoseconds per operation. The -race flag runs all tests through the race detector; always use it in CI.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. testing package: t.Error vs t.Fatal, t.Log, t.Cleanup, t.Helper. 2. Table-driven tests: slice of structs with name/input/expected, t.Run for each case—Go idiomatic standard. 3. testify: assert.Equal (continues on failure) vs. require.Equal (stops test); assert.NoError, require.NotNil. 4. Subtests: t.Run enables parallel subtests, selective filtering with -run=TestFoo/case1. 5. Benchmarks: b.N loop, b.ResetTimer, b.ReportAllocs; interpreting ns/op, B/op, allocs/op. 6. TestMain: os.Exit(m.Run()), global setup (DB migrations) and teardown (container stop). 7. Race flag: go test -race -count=1; catches concurrent map writes, unsynchronised variable access.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: • 'Walk me through how you write a table-driven test in Go.' → []struct{name, input, want}, t.Run loop, t.Parallel() inside each subtest. • 'What's the difference between assert and require in testify?' → assert continues, require stops; use require when subsequent assertions are meaningless after a nil check. • 'How do you run benchmarks and what do you look for?' → go test -bench=. -benchmem; look for unexpected allocations, regression in ns/op across PRs. • 'How do you detect race conditions in your tests?' → go test -race; explain the race detector instruments memory accesses at runtime.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "My standard testing approach in Go is table-driven tests with t.Run for every unit test—it gives you a named, filterable subtest for each case without duplicating setup code. I use require for nil-guards and assert for everything else so failures are clear without stopping unnecessarily. For benchmarks I always pass -benchmem to catch hidden allocations; a spike in allocs/op is often more important than ns/op for latency. Every test in CI runs with -race because the race detector has caught subtle goroutine bugs that code review missed. For integration tests I use TestMain to spin up a real Postgres instance via testcontainers-go and run migrations before m.Run—same binary, no external scripts."
